title: Senior C++ interview
description: Senior-level C++ interview bank (~200 cards) covering ownership, modern C++17/20, concurrency/atomics, low-latency systems, profiling, and system-design topics aligned with a C++ interview study guide.

questions.prompt: Which statement about C++ pointers vs references is correct?

options.text: A reference may be null and rebound later
A pointer stores an address, may be null/uninitialized, and can be reseated
A reference has independent storage identical to a pointer

questions.explanation: References must bind to a valid object and cannot be reseated; pointers hold addresses and may be null.

questions.prompt: What is a key difference between operator new and malloc in C++?

options.text: malloc calls constructors; new does not
new is typed, invokes constructors, and typically throws std::bad_alloc on failure
new returns void* and never throws
malloc computes object size automatically from the type

questions.explanation: new is an operator that constructs objects; malloc is a C function returning void* without constructors.

questions.prompt: Which forms of allocation/construction are valid C++ new expressions?
questions.explanation: C++ has throwing, nothrow, and placement new; there is no standard std::gc new.

questions.prompt: Why is std::make_shared often preferred over shared_ptr<T>(new T)?

options.text: It typically allocates object and control block together and is exception-safer
make_shared makes the pointer unique_ptr-compatible only
shared_ptr(new T) never allocates a control block

questions.explanation: make_shared can do one allocation and avoids leaks if construction throws between new and shared_ptr ownership.

questions.prompt: Which statements about standard smart pointers are correct?

options.text: unique_ptr models exclusive ownership and is move-only
shared_ptr shares ownership via a reference count
weak_ptr participates in ownership and keeps the object alive
auto_ptr is deprecated/removed and should not be used in modern code

questions.explanation: weak_ptr observes without owning; auto_ptr is obsolete.

questions.prompt: What problem does std::weak_ptr primarily solve with shared_ptr graphs?

options.text: It breaks ownership cycles by observing without extending lifetime

questions.explanation: Cycles of shared_ptr leak; weak_ptr breaks the cycle while allowing lock()/expired checks.

questions.prompt: What does RAII mean in modern C++ practice?

options.text: Resources are acquired in constructors and released in destructors tied to object lifetime
All resources must be freed manually in main
Only heap memory may use constructors
Destructors are forbidden for file handles

questions.explanation: RAII binds resource lifetime to object lifetime via ctor/dtor (and move semantics).

questions.prompt: Match each cast to its characteristic.

right.text: Reinterprets the bit pattern / unrelated pointer types

questions.explanation: Prefer C++ casts over C-style casts for intent and safety.

questions.prompt: In C++, what is the language difference between class and struct?

options.text: Default member and base access: private for class, public for struct

questions.explanation: Both can have methods, ctors, and inheritance; defaults differ.

questions.prompt: Why can condition variables not synchronize across separate processes by themselves?

options.text: Processes do not share address space; CV/mutex need shared memory or IPC primitives
Condition variables only work with atomics

questions.explanation: Threads share memory within a process; cross-process sync needs shared memory/IPC.

questions.prompt: Why can a C++ constructor not be virtual?

options.text: During construction the dynamic type/vtable machinery is not yet fully established for virtual dispatch as for normal methods
The standard forbids any factory patterns

questions.explanation: Use cloning/factory idioms instead of virtual constructors; destructors often should be virtual in polymorphic bases.

questions.prompt: Order class relationships from weakest to strongest coupling.
questions.explanation: From temporary use through ownership to type hierarchy — as in the interview notes.

questions.prompt: Match each SOLID letter to its meaning.
questions.explanation: Classic SOLID checklist for design interview answers.

questions.prompt: Which classifications are correct for these patterns?
questions.explanation: Strategy is behavioral; Singleton/Abstract Factory/Builder are creational.

questions.prompt: Runtime polymorphism via virtual functions requires what?

options.text: A hierarchy and virtual dispatch (typically via vtable) selecting the dynamic type
All member functions to be static

questions.explanation: Virtual calls resolve based on dynamic type; templates give compile-time polymorphism.

questions.prompt: If Base::log(const char* = "base") is virtual and Derived overrides with a different default, what prints for Base* p = new Derived(); p->log();?

options.text: Base's default argument text (defaults bind statically to the static type)

questions.explanation: Default arguments are not virtual; the static type of the call site supplies defaults.

questions.prompt: What does explicit on a constructor primarily prevent?

options.text: Implicit converting construction from other types

questions.explanation: explicit blocks surprising implicit conversions; C++20 also has explicit(bool).

questions.prompt: When do you apply the Rule of Five instead of the Rule of Zero?
questions.answerText: When the class directly owns a resource (raw pointer, fd, etc.) not already managed by RAII members, you need a destructor and carefully defined copy/move operations (or =delete). Prefer Rule of Zero by composing unique_ptr/string/vector.
questions.explanation: Interview classic: prefer Zero; Five only for custom resource owners.

questions.prompt: Order typical C++ translation stages from earliest to latest.
questions.explanation: Macros → IR/optimize → asm/object → link libraries.

questions.prompt: What does the One Definition Rule (ODR) require?

options.text: Every entity may be defined arbitrarily often with different bodies
Entities may be declared multiple times but non-inline non-template definitions must appear only once in the program (else ill-formed/UB)

questions.explanation: Duplicate non-inline definitions across TUs violate ODR; inline/templates have special allowances.

questions.prompt: Which may safely have definitions in multiple translation units?

options.text: Non-inline non-static free function defined in two .cpp files identically
Entities in an anonymous namespace (internal linkage per TU)

questions.explanation: Identical non-inline definitions in two TUs are classic ODR bugs.

questions.prompt: What are the two roles of the inline keyword?

options.text: Hint to inline at call sites, and permission for multiple identical definitions across TUs

questions.explanation: Inlining is optional; ODR allowance is the linkage meaning — critical for headers.

questions.prompt: A namespace-scope static variable in a .cpp primarily provides what?

options.text: External linkage visible to all TUs
Internal linkage (not visible to other TUs)

questions.explanation: static at namespace scope → internal linkage (prefer anonymous namespace in modern C++).

questions.prompt: Cross-TU inlining and whole-program opts often need {{flag}} (Link-Time Optimization).
questions.explanation: LTO lets the optimizer see multiple object files together.

questions.prompt: What is Profile-Guided Optimization (PGO)?

options.text: Instrument, run representative workload, rebuild using the profile to guide opts

questions.explanation: PGO + LTO is a common release combo for hot-path layout and branches.

questions.prompt: How does ABI differ from API?

options.text: API is the source-level contract; ABI is the binary calling/layout/mangling contract
API includes register calling conventions only

questions.explanation: Breaking ABI forces client rebuilds even if source still compiles against new headers.

questions.prompt: Match token kinds to examples.
questions.explanation: Lexical analysis splits source into these tokens.

questions.prompt: What does SFINAE mean during template overload resolution?

options.text: Any failure inside a function body is ignored
Substitution failure in a template signature discards that candidate without hard error

questions.explanation: Body errors are hard errors; SFINAE applies to substitution in the signature/declaration.

questions.prompt: In modern C++, what is the preferred readable replacement for many enable_if SFINAE patterns?
questions.explanation: Concepts express constraints clearly; SFINAE remains under the hood/legacy.

questions.prompt: Which are true about POD / trivial / standard-layout ideas?

options.text: Trivial types have defaulted special members and no virtuals in the trivial sense
Standard-layout constrains member access/layout for predictable ABI
std::is_pod is the preferred C++20 trait to use exclusively
POD-ish types are memcpy-friendly for C interop when traits allow

questions.explanation: C++20 deprecates is_pod; check trivial and standard-layout separately.

questions.prompt: Which library utilities arrived (or were standardized prominently) in C++17?
questions.explanation: std::span is C++20; optional/variant/any/string_view/filesystem are C++17 highlights.

questions.prompt: What is the main lifetime risk of std::string_view?

options.text: It always extends temporary lifetime indefinitely
It is non-owning and may dangle if the underlying character sequence dies
It cannot bind to string literals

questions.explanation: Classic bug: string_view v = std::string{"tmp"}; // dangling

questions.prompt: What do structured bindings (C++17) enable?

options.text: Unpacking tuple-like/aggregate objects into named variables
Runtime reflection of all private members

questions.explanation: auto [a,b,c] = tupleOrStruct;

questions.prompt: A C++17 unary right fold summing a pack can be written (args {{op}} ...).
questions.explanation: Fold expressions replace recursive template sum helpers.

questions.prompt: What does if (auto it = m.find(k); it != m.end()) provide?

options.text: An if with init-statement limiting the variable's scope to the if

questions.explanation: C++17 if/switch init keeps temporaries tightly scoped.

questions.prompt: Which attributes are standard and commonly discussed with C++17?
questions.explanation: [[gpu_only]] is not a standard attribute.

questions.prompt: What problem do C++17 inline variables solve?

options.text: Allowing a single definition of a variable in a header included by many TUs

questions.explanation: inline int counter = 0; in a header is ODR-safe across TUs.

questions.prompt: How does std::variant differ from std::any?

options.text: variant is a type-safe union of a fixed alternative set; any can hold any type via type erasure
any is always faster and safer than variant
variant can hold unbounded unknown types without visitation

questions.explanation: Prefer variant when the set is known; any loses static alternatives.

questions.prompt: What is true about a classic C++ union?

options.text: All members are simultaneously active and typed-safe
It overlays storage; only one member should be active; low-level and easy to misuse
It replaces variant entirely in modern code with no downsides
Reading inactive members is always well-defined for all types

questions.explanation: Use std::variant for type-safe discriminated unions.

questions.prompt: What is std::span?

options.text: A non-owning view over a contiguous sequence (pointer+size)

questions.explanation: Like string_view but for arbitrary contiguous elements.

questions.prompt: What does std::format provide vs printf-style formatting?
questions.explanation: Format strings are checked more safely than %d mismatches.

questions.prompt: Which statements about std::ranges are correct?

options.text: Algorithms can take whole ranges instead of iterator pairs
views compose lazily with | without always building intermediate containers
ranges::sort requires a C-style array only

questions.explanation: Ranges modernize <algorithm> usage and lazy pipelines.

questions.prompt: What do C++20 concepts primarily express?

options.text: Compile-time constraints on template parameters with clear diagnostics

questions.explanation: requires expressions document and enforce capabilities.

questions.prompt: Match C++20 keywords to meaning.

right.text: May run at compile time or runtime
Must run at compile time (immediate function)
Must have static initialization; object need not be const

questions.explanation: Common interview trio from the notes.

questions.prompt: What happens if you call a consteval function with a runtime-only argument?

options.text: It falls back to runtime silently

questions.explanation: Immediate functions require constant-expression arguments.

questions.prompt: Why may const int x = runtime_value; still be unusable as a consteval argument?

options.text: const is not sufficient; the initializer must itself be a constant expression

questions.explanation: Integral const with constant initializer can be a constant expression; runtime init is not.

questions.prompt: Which are C++20 features?
questions.explanation: auto_ptr stays dead.

questions.prompt: C++20 exposes native endianness via std::{{name}} in <bit>.
questions.explanation: Compare std::endian::native to big/little.

questions.prompt: For uint32_t x = 0x01020304, little-endian machines typically have which first byte?
questions.explanation: LSB first on little-endian (x86/x64, most ARM).

questions.prompt: Which are classic multithreading hazards?
questions.explanation: All appear in the interview notes' thread-risk list.

questions.prompt: What happens if std::thread is destroyed while joinable?

options.text: It detaches automatically and continues safely

questions.explanation: Always join or detach before destruction.

questions.prompt: Why specify std::launch::async with std::async for true concurrency?

options.text: Default policy may defer execution until get()/wait(), possibly running synchronously
Without it, code will not compile

questions.explanation: Be explicit when you need a new thread of execution.

questions.prompt: Why is volatile not a substitute for std::atomic in threading?

options.text: volatile does not provide atomicity or inter-thread synchronization semantics
volatile prevents all optimizations including register allocation forever across threads by standard sync

questions.explanation: Use atomics/mutexes for concurrency; volatile is for special memory-mapped IO cases.

questions.prompt: Match memory_order to role.

right.text: Atomicity only; no sync with other locations

questions.explanation: Hot paths often use deliberate acquire/release instead of seq_cst.

questions.prompt: In an SPSC ring buffer, why store the producer index with memory_order_release after writing the slot?

options.text: To make the payload stores visible to a consumer that acquire-loads the index
Because release makes the index larger numerically
Release is required for single-threaded code

questions.explanation: Payload first, then release-store the index; consumer acquire-loads then reads payload.

questions.prompt: What is false sharing?

options.text: Two threads sharing a mutex correctly
Threads mutating independent variables that share a cache line, causing ping-pong coherence traffic

questions.explanation: Pad/align hot atomics (e.g. head/tail) onto separate cache lines.

questions.prompt: Sketch what an interviewer expects in a simplified shared_ptr implementation.
questions.answerText: Separate control block with use_count; copy increments; destructor/assignment decrements and deletes object+block at 0; move steals without touching count; handle self-assignment and empty nullptr without allocating a count; note real shared_ptr uses atomics, weak_count, aliasing ctor, custom deleters, and make_shared one-allocation.
questions.explanation: Classic coding interview from the notes.

questions.prompt: Why is the real std::shared_ptr control block reference count atomic?

options.text: To allow copying across threads without data races on the count
Atomics make the managed T automatically thread-safe

questions.explanation: Shared ownership can cross threads; T still needs its own synchronization.

questions.prompt: After std::string b = std::move(a); what is true of a?

options.text: a is valid but unspecified; safe to assign/destroy; do not assume contents

questions.explanation: Moved-from requires valid state, not a specific value.

questions.prompt: Which are undefined behavior in C++?

options.text: Data race on non-atomic shared memory

questions.explanation: Throwing user types is fine; the others are classic UB.

questions.prompt: Order events for a block-scope object lifetime.
questions.explanation: Lifetime brackets successful initialization through destructor start.

questions.prompt: Order construction of a derived object.
questions.explanation: Destruction reverses this order.

questions.prompt: Perfect forwarding uses std::{{fn}} on a forwarding reference T&&.
questions.explanation: std::move unconditionally casts to rvalue; forward preserves value category.

questions.prompt: Prefer v.{{m}}(...) to construct in-place in a vector when it avoids an extra temporary.
questions.explanation: emplace_back forwards args to the element constructor.

questions.prompt: What does the Rule of Zero recommend?

options.text: Always write all five special members
Prefer types that manage no raw resources so special members can be defaulted/omitted
Delete copy and also delete move always

questions.explanation: Compose RAII members and let the compiler generate special members.

questions.prompt: In trading/low-latency systems, what is optimized beyond average throughput?

options.text: Predictable response time with emphasis on tail latency (p99/p99.9) and jitter

questions.explanation: Determinism: avoid alloc/locks/syscalls on the hot path.

questions.prompt: What is p99 latency?

options.text: The latency threshold at the 99th percentile — 99% of samples are ≤ that value

questions.explanation: Tail percentiles expose spikes that averages hide.

questions.prompt: Which techniques appear in low-latency C++ systems?

options.text: Kernel bypass NICs for extreme networking
JSON parsing on every tick as the preferred wire format

questions.explanation: Prefer fixed layouts/SBE/FlatBuffers over JSON on critical path.

questions.prompt: Why is Structure-of-Arrays often better for SIMD than Array-of-Structures?

options.text: AoS packs better for scalar random access always
SoA keeps like-fields contiguous, improving vector loads and cache behavior for bulk ops

questions.explanation: Contiguous homogeneous lanes vectorize cleanly.

questions.prompt: What helps effective SIMD?

options.text: Avoiding hard-to-predict branches in hot loops
Heavy pointer-chasing linked lists as the primary layout

questions.explanation: Linked lists defeat vector loads.

questions.prompt: Match tool to use case.

right.text: Visualize where CPU time concentrates in stacks

questions.explanation: Measure before optimizing; Valgrind tools are heavy.

questions.prompt: How should telemetry interact with a low-latency hot path?

options.text: Synchronously flush every metric on the critical path
Keep instrumentation off the hot path: async queues, sampling, batching
Use malloc per event on the order path

questions.explanation: Measure without becoming the bottleneck.

questions.prompt: Which statement about -O flags is most accurate for production low-latency builds?

options.text: -O2/-O3 with careful flags, often plus LTO/PGO, after measuring

questions.explanation: Choose based on benchmarks; -O0 is for debug.

questions.prompt: How can real-time video pipeline work map to low-latency interview language?
questions.answerText: Frame it as minimizing action-to-frame latency and tail jank: hot-path transmux (Annex B), buffer reuse, seek/decode pipeline sync, play/pause state machine trading time-to-first-frame vs underruns — same mindset as trading: identify critical path, measure, remove stalls/allocs, validate with telemetry.
questions.explanation: Narrative bridge from the notes — not HFT, same engineering habits.

questions.prompt: For ~1000 document uploads/sec needing OCR, why is synchronous OCR-in-request a bad default?

options.text: OCR is typically too slow/CPU-heavy; it would destroy API latency and capacity

questions.explanation: Upload fast + async workers is the standard pattern.

questions.prompt: Which design choices fit a high-ingest OCR pipeline?

options.text: Presigned upload to object storage + job id
Separate lanes for tiny images vs giant PDFs to avoid head-of-line blocking
Run multi-second OCR inside the load balancer request thread

questions.explanation: Chunk huge PDFs; scale workers on queue lag.

questions.prompt: What is head-of-line blocking in a heterogeneous OCR queue?

options.text: A giant PDF job delaying many small jobs behind it in one shared queue

questions.explanation: Route by size/pages into fast/normal/heavy pools.

questions.prompt: Order a sensible OCR ingest flow.
questions.explanation: Separate ingest ACK from heavy compute.

questions.prompt: gRPC typically uses HTTP/2 and {{codec}} contracts.
questions.explanation: Strong typing and streaming; still often too heavy for HFT wire paths.

questions.prompt: In template<typename T> void f(T&& x), what is T&&?

options.text: A forwarding/universal reference that may bind lvalues or rvalues depending on deduction

questions.explanation: Collapsing rules + std::forward enable perfect forwarding.

questions.prompt: What does =delete on a special member mean?

options.text: The member is defined as deleted — using it is ill-formed

questions.explanation: Common for non-copyable types alongside unique_ptr members.

questions.prompt: When should a base class destructor usually be virtual?

options.text: When deleting derived objects through base pointers (polymorphic ownership)
Only if the class has no members

questions.explanation: Non-virtual base dtor + delete via base* is UB if destructor nontrivial path needed.

questions.prompt: Which complexity claims are correct for typical std:: containers?
questions.explanation: std::list is O(n) for random access.

questions.prompt: After vector reallocation, what happens to prior iterators/pointers/references into it?
questions.explanation: Capacity growth moves storage — classic footgun.

questions.prompt: Why mark move constructors noexcept when possible?

options.text: vector and other containers can use moves during growth instead of falling back to copies
It is required for all functions

questions.explanation: std::move_if_noexcept / vector strong exception guarantee interactions.

questions.prompt: What is Argument-Dependent Lookup (ADL) mainly used for?

options.text: Finding free functions (e.g. swap, operators) in associated namespaces of argument types

questions.explanation: Also why using std::swap; swap(a,b); is an idiom.

questions.prompt: What is a primary benefit of the Pimpl idiom?

options.text: Faster compile times / ABI stability by hiding private implementation

questions.explanation: Trade an allocation/indirection for encapsulation and firewalled headers.

questions.prompt: Which are true about copy elision / NRVO?

options.text: Compilers may omit copies/moves of temporaries under the rules
NRVO targets named locals returned by value
Elision means RAII destructors never run for any object
Since C++17, some prvalue elision is mandatory

questions.explanation: Destructors still run for the eventual object; elision skips intermediate temporaries.

questions.prompt: What does a disengaged std::optional represent?

options.text: Absence of a value without a separate bool flag object

questions.explanation: Check has_value()/operator bool before value().

questions.prompt: Why might seq_cst be avoided on a hot SPSC queue index update?

options.text: It is the strongest ordering and may be more expensive than needed acquire/release pair

questions.explanation: Use the weakest correct order; measure.

questions.prompt: What is the practical guidance on memory_order_consume?

options.text: It is subtle/rarely used correctly; prefer acquire in practice

questions.explanation: Notes: treat consume as academic; use acquire.

questions.prompt: Condition variables require waiting with what?

options.text: A predicate loop and a mutex (unique_lock), to handle spurious wakeups

questions.explanation: while (!ready) cv.wait(lock);

questions.prompt: Which statements are careful/correct?

options.text: Lock-free structures still need correct memory ordering
ABA problems can affect CAS loops

questions.explanation: Lock-free ≠ free of atomics or design bugs.

questions.prompt: Typical x86 cache line size relevant to false sharing padding is often:
questions.explanation: Pad hot counters to 64B boundaries as a common heuristic.

questions.prompt: Why prefer filesystem APIs taking std::error_code in production services?

options.text: They avoid exceptions on failure paths, aiding control in tight/reliable code
Exceptions are removed from the language

questions.explanation: Throwing overloads still exist; choose per error strategy.

questions.prompt: What problem does std::invoke unify?

options.text: Calling functions, member pointers, and functors with one protocol

questions.explanation: Used internally by std::thread/bind/apply-style utilities.

questions.prompt: C++ name lookup uses which scoping model?

options.text: Dynamic scope via call stack only
Lexical/static scope based on nesting in source

questions.explanation: Dynamic scope is not a C++ feature.

questions.prompt: Why is using namespace std; in a header discouraged?

options.text: It pollutes the global namespace of every translation unit that includes it

questions.explanation: Prefer targeted using declarations in .cpp scopes.

questions.prompt: Match abbreviations to meanings.
questions.explanation: From the notes glossary — jitter sources in managed runtimes.

questions.prompt: For ultra-low-latency market data, why avoid JSON on the hot path?

options.text: Parsing/allocation/jitter vs fixed-layout binary schemas (e.g. SBE)
Binary protocols cannot cross a network

questions.explanation: Deterministic schemas beat text parsing under μs budgets.

questions.prompt: What is a hot path vs cold path split?

options.text: Keep latency-critical work free of logging/alloc/IO; push bookkeeping elsewhere
Run cold code on GPU only

questions.explanation: Trading engines: order path vs reporting/telemetry.

questions.prompt: How do you correctly manage a dynamic array with unique_ptr?

options.text: unique_ptr<T[]> or unique_ptr<T, void(*)(T*)> with delete[] deleter

questions.explanation: Array form or custom deleter; plain unique_ptr<T> uses delete.

questions.prompt: When is enable_shared_from_this needed?

options.text: To safely create shared_ptr to this from a member function when already owned by shared_ptr

questions.explanation: Avoid shared_ptr(this) which creates an independent control block.

questions.prompt: What does shared_ptr's aliasing constructor allow?

options.text: shared_ptr that shares ownership with another but points to a subobject

questions.explanation: Useful for pointers into members while keeping parent alive.

questions.prompt: A const member function may:

options.text: Modify mutable members and call other const methods; not non-mutable non-static data

questions.explanation: Bit-level const with mutable escape hatch.

questions.prompt: Typical legitimate use of mutable?

options.text: Caching/lazy fields in logically const methods, or mutexes for const thread-safe reads

questions.explanation: Logical constness vs bitwise constness.

questions.prompt: Why make operator bool explicit?

options.text: Avoid unintended implicit conversions in arithmetic/overload resolution
To allow if(x) only via static_cast always failing

questions.explanation: Contextual conversions still allow if (ptr).

questions.prompt: What does final on a virtual method do?

options.text: Prevents further overriding in derived classes

questions.explanation: Also final on a class seals inheritance.

questions.prompt: Why use override?

options.text: Compiler checks you actually override a virtual; catches signature mismatches

questions.explanation: Without it, silent new overload bugs.

questions.prompt: What is object slicing?

options.text: Assigning/passing derived by value as base, dropping derived parts
Linking only half an object file

questions.explanation: Prefer references/pointers/smart pointers to polymorphic objects.

questions.prompt: A polymorphic object typically stores what extra per-instance data?

options.text: A vptr (pointer to vtable) on common ABIs
A copy of all base classes' source

questions.explanation: Plus possible multiple vptrs with MI.

questions.prompt: How does C++ address the diamond inheritance problem?

options.text: Virtual inheritance to share a single base subobject

questions.explanation: virtual public Base.

questions.prompt: CRTP is mainly used for:

options.text: Static polymorphism / mixin behavior without virtual calls

questions.explanation: template<class D> struct Base { ... static_cast<D*>(this) ... }.

questions.prompt: std::function is an example of:

options.text: Type erasure of callable objects with potential allocation/overhead

questions.explanation: Know allocation/SBO tradeoffs in interviews.

questions.prompt: What is SBO/SSO?

options.text: Small buffer/string optimization storing short data in-object to avoid heap

questions.explanation: std::string / some function impls.

questions.prompt: Which standard type is move-only?
questions.explanation: shared_ptr is copyable; string_view is copyable non-owning.

questions.prompt: Why is vector<bool> special/problematic?

options.text: It is a space-optimized proxy container, not a regular container of bool objects

questions.explanation: Proxies break pointer/reference assumptions.

questions.prompt: After moving a std::string, why might it still look non-empty on some impls?

options.text: Moved-from is unspecified; SSO may leave a non-empty valid string
Move must clear always by standard for string

questions.explanation: Do not rely on empty-after-move for string.

questions.prompt: std::launder is related to:

options.text: Lifetime/placement-new and pointer provenance when storage is reused

questions.explanation: Advanced lifetime topic for seniors.

questions.prompt: C++23 start_lifetime_as helps with:

options.text: Explicitly starting object lifetimes on raw storage (e.g. networking buffers)

questions.explanation: Replaces some launder/reinterpret patterns carefully.

questions.prompt: std::bit_cast (C++20) provides:

options.text: Safe value-preserving reinterpretation between trivially copyable types of equal size

questions.explanation: Better than memcpy hacks for type punning when allowed.

questions.prompt: Why care about alignment for SIMD loads?

options.text: Misaligned accesses may be slower or fault depending on ISA/API
Alignment never matters on any CPU

questions.explanation: aligned_alloc / alignas / assume_aligned.

questions.prompt: How can branches hurt low-latency loops?

options.text: Mispredicts flush pipelines; data-dependent branches add jitter

questions.explanation: Prefer branchless techniques carefully after measuring.

questions.prompt: Why avoid syscalls on the trading hot path?

options.text: User/kernel transitions and kernel work add large unpredictable latency
Syscalls run in SIMD registers only

questions.explanation: Batch IO; kernel bypass for extremes.

questions.prompt: Why do page faults matter in latency-sensitive code?

options.text: Demand paging on first touch causes multi-μs/ms stalls

questions.explanation: Warm up / mlock / prefault critical arenas.

questions.prompt: Pinning threads to cores helps by:

options.text: Reducing migrations and stabilizing cache locality

questions.explanation: Common HFT ops practice with isolation.

questions.prompt: Huge pages can help latency by:

options.text: Reducing TLB misses for large working sets

questions.explanation: Trade memory fragmentation/ops complexity.

questions.prompt: Why prefer bounded queues in backpressured systems?

options.text: Finite capacity forces load shedding/blocking instead of unbounded RAM growth

questions.explanation: Pair with drop/slow-down policies.

questions.prompt: Why is SPSC simpler/faster than MPMC?

options.text: Single producer/consumer avoids CAS contention on shared indices

questions.explanation: Shard into SPSC lanes when possible.

questions.prompt: Acquire/release establish what relationship?

options.text: Synchronizes-with / happens-before edges for visibility of prior writes

questions.explanation: Core of the C++ memory model.

questions.prompt: A data race is:

options.text: Concurrent conflicting non-atomic accesses with at least one write, without sync — UB

questions.explanation: Atomics or mutexes remove the race.

questions.prompt: Which are true about move semantics?

options.text: Moves can transfer resources instead of deep-copying
std::move is a cast to rvalue, not a move by itself
Moved-from objects may be reused after assignment
Move always zeros all bytes of the source
